title: Understanding Emotions

learn.summary: Emotions are data, not directives: signals about needs, threats, and values, built by the brain partly from context and past experience (Lisa Feldman Barrett's constructed-emotion theory). The skill stack is: notice, name precisely, decode the message, choose the response. People who do this well — high 'emotional granularity' — show better regulation and health outcomes.

do: Set two random phone alarms daily for three days. At each, name your current emotion with one precise word and what it might be signaling.

children.title: Affect Labeling

learn.summary: Matthew Lieberman's UCLA studies show that putting feelings into words dampens amygdala response and engages prefrontal regulation — 'name it to tame it' (Dan Siegel's phrase) is real neuroscience, not a slogan. The effect works even though people predict labeling will make them feel worse. It is the cheapest regulation tool in existence: one honest sentence.

do: Next strong emotion this week, say or write one plain sentence: 'I am feeling ___ right now.' Rate intensity before and after naming.

children.title: Emotional Granularity

learn.summary: Barrett's research finds people who distinguish 'irritated' from 'resentful' from 'depleted' (instead of one big 'bad') regulate better, drink less under stress, and are less likely to lash out — precision creates options, because each specific emotion suggests a different remedy. Granularity is trainable: exposure to finer-grained emotion vocabulary measurably improves it. 'Stressed' is usually a low-resolution label for something more actionable.

do: Ban the words 'stressed' and 'fine' from your self-descriptions for one week; force a more precise word every time.

children.title: Emotions as Data

learn.summary: Each emotion family carries a rough message: anger flags a violated boundary or blocked goal, anxiety flags an uncertain future needing preparation, sadness flags loss needing processing, guilt flags a values breach, envy flags something you want. Treating emotions as sensor readings — sometimes miscalibrated, always informative — beats both suppression (rebound effects) and blind obedience. Read the gauge; then decide, with your values, whether to act.

do: Take your most persistent recent emotion and write two sentences: what is it flagging, and is the sensor accurate or miscalibrated here?

children.title: Urge Surfing

learn.summary: Alan Marlatt's relapse-prevention technique treats cravings and urges as waves: they rise, crest, and fall within roughly 20–30 minutes if not fed. Instead of fighting or obeying the urge, you observe it with curiosity — where it sits in the body, how it changes — until it passes. Originally built for addiction, it works on any impulse: doomscrolling, snapping at someone, stress-eating.

do: Pick one habitual urge (checking your phone, a snack, a sharp reply). Once this week, set a 10-minute timer and just watch the urge instead of acting. Note what happens to its intensity.
